## The beat stays put; the note inside it moves

Straight eighth notes cut each beat into two equal halves. *Swing* leaves the
beat boundary where it was and moves the cut: the first span grows, the second
shrinks to match. Bar length never changes. You get a recurring long-short
pair.

The `amount` parameter below controls that displacement. At zero the two sleeps
are `0.5` and `0.5`. At `0.16` they become `0.66` and `0.34`, near a
two-thirds/one-third split. At `0.33` they reach `0.83` and `0.17`. Listen to
that last pass twice. Does it still read to you as swing, or has it turned into
a plain dotted rhythm?

*Microtiming* covers the smaller onset deviations underneath the written grid.
This program adds bounded, seeded jitter to timing and to amplitude. Swing is
the systematic displacement; jitter is the wobble around it. Every random draw
happens at the top of the pair, before anything uses it, and the reason for
that turns out to matter.

## Three amounts over one bar

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_random_seed 42
use_bpm 96
use_synth :piano

define :swing_bar do |amount, jitter, amp_spread|
  4.times do
    # Draw everything here, in a fixed order, used or not.
    timing_offset = rrand(-jitter, jitter)
    first_amp_offset = rrand(-0.05, 0.05)
    second_amp_offset = rrand(-0.05, 0.05)

    late = amount + timing_offset
    play :c4, amp: 0.85 + first_amp_offset * amp_spread, release: 0.15
    sleep 0.5 + late
    play :g4, amp: 0.7 + second_amp_offset * amp_spread, release: 0.15
    sleep 0.5 - late
  end
  sleep 1
end

[0.0, 0.16, 0.33].each { |amount| swing_bar amount, 0.01, 1.0 }
```

The first pass keeps every C-G pair close to even. Through the later passes G
slides progressively later inside its beat. One `late` value gets added to the
first sleep and subtracted from the second, so the C that follows still lands
on the next quarter-note boundary. Tap the beat and you'll feel it stay put.

## Sweep the amount, then the jitter

1. Compare `0.16` against `0.33` on their own. Tap the quarter note and ignore
   the individual notes. The first gives you a moderate lilt; the second states
   the long-short proportion outright.

2. Restore all three amounts and raise jitter from `0.01` to `0.08`. Watch the
   quarter-note boundaries and mark where they stop feeling solid. Describe
   what you heard without deciding it sounds human.

3. Restore the jitter and change the final argument from `1.0` to `0`. The
   attacks now vary only in placement. Compare that with the original, where a
   louder note pulls attention onto a timing deviation you'd otherwise skate
   past.

## Why hoisting the draws makes variation 3 honest

That third variation is the reason the random values are drawn into named
variables at the top of the loop. `use_random_seed 42` reproduces one stream of
numbers in one order. Delete an `rrand` call and every later draw in the stream
slides up to fill the gap, so a comparison meant to isolate amplitude quietly
changes the timing too. Two things move, and you learn nothing from either.

Multiplying by `amp_spread` keeps all three draws in the stream and stops the
last two from reaching the output. Same numbers, same order, same timing
jitter, and only amplitude has changed. Make it a habit in seeded programs:
draw first into names, decide afterwards what to use. Three extra lines buy you
a controlled comparison.

## Why the sum of a swung pair is still one beat

Swing is a deterministic transformation of paired durations. Add `late` to the
first half, subtract it from the second, and their sum is one beat whatever
`late` was. The inner onset moves freely; every following pair starts where it
always did.

The jitter could have broken that and doesn't, for the same reason. One
`timing_offset` feeds one `late`, which appears with opposite signs, so each
jittered pair still sums to one. Bounds still matter. A large enough value
collapses one of the two durations or shoves the inner attack against a
boundary. Keep the perturbation far under your shortest subdivision.

There's no correct swing percentage. Players and styles use different
proportions, and one player changes them with tempo. The sweep is a listening
map, with no ranking in it.

Read timing and amplitude separately. A louder event seems earlier and more
important even when its onset never moved, so zeroing the amplitude spread is
what leaves the timing effect standing alone.

Beat values become milliseconds only through tempo. At 120 BPM, `0.01` beats is
5 milliseconds; at 60 BPM it's 10. Jitter here is written in beats, so the
physical deviation grows as you slow down. For a fixed physical delay, convert
with `milliseconds * bpm / 60000.0` and say in a comment why.

Lesson 17 swaps displaced pairs for two exact subdivisions running at once. The
shared cycle boundary again prevents drift, and each layer divides the span by
a different count.

## A clap-back drill

Build a hidden four-beat pattern from `0.5` and `1.0` durations. Validate the
array before anything sounds, play it once, leave four beats for a clap-back,
and print the array only after that window closes.

Keep it straight until the prompt, the pause and the reveal are reproducible.
Then swing the paired eighths without changing the four-beat total, hoisting
your draws so one seed serves both versions. Audition both in Sonic Pi 5. Your
code proves the sums; your notes should describe onset placement and stop short
of claiming that randomised variation reproduces a human player.
